footnote.text: There’s going to be endless free energy.

brief.head: Power, not bombs
brief.text: Twenty-four countries have nuclear power and have never built a bomb, Amit Varma said. The two were fused in the 1970s peace and environmental movements. {078-C02}

brief.head: Three sources of risk
brief.text: Radioactive material that travels thousands of kilometres, runaway chain reactions and complex systems where small human errors grow: Ajay Shah’s three sources of nuclear risk. {078-C03}

brief.head: The sun clocks off
brief.text: Solar is unbeatable while the sun shines, Ajay Shah said, but it sets just as people get home. Investors who doubt storage can bet on nuclear. {078-C09}

brief.head: Blame the driver
brief.text: Indian law makes a reactor’s vendor liable forever, Ajay Shah said, so no global vendor will sell. Like a car, a reactor should become the operator’s responsibility after handover. {078-C11}

brief.head: Between friends
brief.text: By Ajay Shah’s sums, a 50 MW plant serves about 25,000 households. He rounded a home’s 2,000 watts down to 1,000, because “we don’t want pesky little details”. {078-J06}

thought.text: You face a problem, that doesn’t mean you stop. It means you try harder.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah make the nuclear case
lead.head: Set the atom free
body: Nuclear power has grown up under a dark cloud, Amit Varma argued, but the facts are completely different. “Nuclear energy is the safest form of energy known to man,” he said. {078-C01}

Three Mile Island killed no one. At Fukushima, people died because of the tsunami and a hurried evacuation, not because of the nuclear mishap. Chernobyl did kill people, though the numbers are disputed.
Even on the most negative estimate, Varma said, fewer people have died in sixty years of nuclear energy than in a month of accidents related to coal.

France, he said, gets 71 per cent of its power from nuclear energy, has had no safety issues and has brought costs down dramatically. Sixty years of nuclear waste could fit in an underground bunker the size of a Walmart.

Why, then, has the world held back? Ajay Shah, reporting work done with his co-author Akshay Jaitly, named two reasons, fear and cost, and argued that both have largely been solved or are within reach of being solved.
## Counting the dead

On fear, Shah asked for a sense of proportion. Adding nuclear power means adding some nuclear risk to the world and removing some coal risk, and coal is the dirtiest source of all, on pollution, carbon dioxide and deaths.

Count excess deaths per megawatt-hour, he said, and nuclear wins. Spectacular accidents, like plane crashes, make headlines, and that is “messing with our ability to do probabilistic reasoning”. {078-C04}
Safety, Shah argued, is an engineering problem. The three famous accidents all involved first-generation designs, and many newer reactors shut themselves down when something goes wrong.
## A reactor in a crate
On cost, his answer came from the assembly line. A large plant of 2,000 or 4,000 megawatts takes twenty years to build, and only a handful will ever be made, so it never gets cheaper.
“How do you get the price of a nuclear reactor down?” Shah asked. “The answer is industrialisation.” {078-C07}
A small modular reactor of 50 or 100 megawatts, about the size of a big truck, could be made by the thousand, arrive in a crate and be switched on like a factory’s diesel generator.
Meta and Google, Varma noted, had just placed big orders for such reactors. “We are beyond the world of theory,” he said.
## Freedom to choose
In India, Shah said, everything nuclear has been treated as the business of the Department of Atomic Energy, and nuclear’s share of the country’s energy has stayed minuscule.

He set out five conditions for change: freedom for private Indians to import plants; freedom to sell power directly to industrial and commercial buyers; CISF security on the airport model; compliance with the International Atomic Energy Agency’s standards; and a fix to civil nuclear liability law. {078-C10}
The hosts, Varma stressed, “have not made an argument for action. We have made an argument for freedom.” {078-C12}

Private players should weigh solar, wind, storage and nuclear by their own logic. If the government truly regulated for safety, Varma added, it would mandate nuclear power, and the hosts did not want that either.

Could India, short of what Shah calls invisible infrastructure, manage any of this, Varma asked. Shah admitted the path would be difficult. “I have no illusions that there’s a smooth path to these five things,” he said.

second.label: Fukushima, 2011
second.head: If Japan, why not us?
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the meeting that turned Germany against nuclear power
body: After Chernobyl, Ajay Shah said, a liberal democracy could tell itself that the disaster was a Soviet failure, and that a free society would make better decisions. Fukushima, in 2011, ended that comfort.

Angela Merkel, then head of Germany, called a meeting after Fukushima around one sentence: the Japanese are as good as us; if a nuclear accident happened there, can it happen here? {#merkel} Merkel, he noted, has a PhD in chemistry and could reason about probabilities.

The German logic was simple. Germans saw themselves as better engineers than the Soviets, but not better than the Japanese. {078-S01} Germany decided to shut down all its nuclear energy, and seen from 2024, Shah said, that was not such a great decision.

quote.text: So if an accident could happen in Japan, could it happen in Germany?

second.caption: Angela Merkel’s Fukushima question

third.head: Fear has a body count
body: Not using nuclear energy can cost lives, Amit Varma argued. He recalled Ajay Shah’s point, made before recording: after Fukushima, the reactor was shut down and Japan shifted to coal, and there were deaths because of that. {078-S06}
“So actually it wasn’t the nuclear energy per se or that accident that caused deaths,” Varma said. “It was then stopping to use it, getting carried away that caused further deaths.”

He added a fact he half-remembered. After 9/11, when security measures went up and people were scared, they drove more and flew less, and mortality went up, because more people die in car accidents than in plane crashes, by an order of magnitude.
Shah had made a related point earlier: plane crashes make headlines, but flying from Bombay to Delhi is far safer than driving. {078-C04}
third.caption: the deaths caused by fear

p2.title: The nuclear option
p2.deck: Fear, cost and the Indian state: the hosts walk through what went wrong, and what India must change

sections.label: The history
sections.head: Endless energy, endless delays
sections.caption: why nuclear power stumbled
body: In 1945, Ajay Shah said, the mood was a boundless optimism that humanity had figured out the whole thing and there would be endless free energy. In practice, nuclear energy has been a disappointment worldwide.

It proved extremely capital intensive, partly because the equipment is expensive and partly because of delays in construction. A modern large plant of two or four thousand megawatts takes twenty years to build. {#twentyyears} Add up the economics, Shah said, and it looks terrible.
## Blame the system

Then came the fear. When Chernobyl happened, many people explained it away as the monumental stupidity and systemic failure of the Soviet Union, where people afraid of being sent to Siberia kept making wrong decisions. “Authoritarian systems make people stupid and they make mistakes,” as Shah put it. {078-C06}

He pointed to HBO’s *Chernobyl* as a textbook account of how a big oppressive state fails, with nothing to do with nuclear power. The Soviets, he added, never really figured out aircraft carriers or submarines either.
The hope that a liberal democracy would do better lasted until Fukushima in 2011, which shook even Angela Merkel’s Germany into shutting down all its nuclear energy.

~ This, for Shah, is the crisis of nuclear energy: a boundless source of power that fails hard dollars-and-cents calculations, with the looming problem of safety on top. The hosts argue that both problems are largely solved or within reach.

quote.text: We are not better engineers than the Japanese. We are better engineers than the Soviets.

sections.label: Safety
sections.head: The real killer is coal
sections.caption: the safety of nuclear reactors
body: Ajay Shah went back to first principles. Three things, he said, came together in the famous disasters. Radioactive material is a different game: a gas release travels thousands of kilometres, comes down as radioactive rain and triggers birth defects.

A runaway chain reaction can melt hundreds of metres into the ground and contaminate groundwater. And a reactor is a complex system, where a human error can magnify into something much bigger. {078-C03}
Even so, count sixty years of excess deaths and the numbers are modest. “The killer is coal,” Shah said, “and you haven’t even started counting climate change yet.”
## Unsafe at any speed
Nor are these problems fixed for ever. In 1965, Shah recalled, Ralph Nader’s *Unsafe at Any Speed* documented the dangers of American cars, and revolutionary gains in car safety followed. {078-J13}
Many improved reactor designs simply shut themselves down in a safety incident, as forces like gravity pull the fissile material apart. There can be no runaway chain reaction. {078-C05}
~ The proof, Shah said, is already at sea: the reactors on the aircraft carriers and submarines of advanced economies have run for decades without a safety incident.

quote.text: This is the heart of the idea that it’s about clever engineering.

sections.label: Small reactors
sections.head: Reactors off the assembly line
sections.caption: small modular reactors
body: To show how nuclear power can get cheap, Ajay Shah went back to the Second World War, when assembly-line ships beat the U-boats and mass-produced Sherman tanks overwhelmed the Tiger. Scale and learning, he argued, beat craftsmanship.

A 4,000 megawatt reactor will only ever be made in a handful, he said, so it cannot be industrialised. At 50 or 100 megawatts you can think of making a thousand, or ten thousand, with every component mass-produced. {078-C07}
Such a reactor, about 30 per cent bigger than the biggest truck, would come in a crate. Place it on site, throw a switch, and it runs like the diesel gen sets so many Indian factories already have.
## The solar precedent

Solar, Shah said, has had one of the greatest cost collapses in world history, because its manufacturing has just two simple steps. The first, polysilicon, is a scale business: “There are only ten factories in the world who do this at scale.” {#tenfactories}
~ Amit Varma spotted an irony. “This is an artisanal show. We are both artisans,” he said, and here was Shah telling everyone not to do important things the artisanal way. {078-J05}

quote.text: And if there is to be any future in nuclear, it will come because of manufacturing that will crash prices of SMRs.

sections.label: The Indian story
sections.head: Power plants are a business
sections.caption: nuclear power as a business
body: Just as in space research, Ajay Shah said, India assumed that nuclear work could only be done by the government. That was debatable even in 1945 or 1955. Today it is very wrong.

He wants weapons and energy decoupled. Steel for guns and artillery shells is a defence business, where strategic autonomy matters. In energy, India is a normal part of globalisation: Bharat Heavy Electricals makes generation equipment, but imported equipment competes with it.

Nuclear power should work the same way. L&T could ask whether to make small reactors for the world market; Tata Power or Reliance Energy could buy a nuclear generating station; Hindalco could buy a French reactor for captive power. “It is congenitally not possible for the Indian State to do anything efficiently,” Shah said. {078-C08}
## A share that never grew

The government approach, he said, has not worked: nuclear’s share of Indian energy consumption is minuscule and has not grown. He made the same case against handing digital public goods to a public sector company.
~ Amit Varma recommended Jahnavi Phalkey’s *Atomic State*, on the early pioneers of nuclear science in India, and his conversation with her, *Jahnavi and the Cyclotron*. {078-R05}

quote.text: Building nuclear reactors is a business. It’s a normal private business with some interplay with the government

sections.label: Five conditions
sections.head: Five knots to untie
sections.caption: five conditions for nuclear freedom
body: Ajay Shah listed five problems the Indian state must work on. The first: private Indians must be free to decide to import a nuclear plant. {078-C10}
A 50 megawatt plant, he said, costs about two to three hundred million dollars, or Rs 1,500 to 2,500 crore, within the means of India’s top hundred companies.

Second, owners must be free to sell power directly to industrial and commercial buyers, keeping out the distribution companies, which think nuclear too expensive. Offshore wind developers already have that freedom.

Third, security on the airport model. Private airlines fly in and out of private airports, while the government runs aviation security. At nuclear plants, the CISF would guard the uranium and the waste under clear protocols, at the operator’s cost. {#cisf}
## Who answers for accidents
Fourth, India must sign up to and comply with the International Atomic Energy Agency’s standards, or the world will not sell it fuel and reactors.

Fifth, liability. After you buy a car, the brakes are your responsibility. Under the international doctrine, victims sue only the operator, who alone may sue the vendor over a design defect. {078-C11}
~ Indian law instead makes the vendor liable forever, and so, Shah said, no global firm will sell a reactor to an Indian buyer.

quote.text: There’s a handover date, and then responsibility shifts to the operator.

sections.label: The argument
sections.head: Permission, not a push
sections.caption: freedom, not action
body: Amit Varma drew the threads together. The hosts were not telling private companies to go and invest in nuclear, nor the Indian state to solve the power problem. They asked only that the state stop shutting it out. {078-C12}
It is not the job of thinkers or policymakers, Ajay Shah had said, to plan centrally that there will be 5,000 megawatts of nuclear. {#central}

Varma had added a twist earlier. If the government really regulated on safety grounds, it would mandate nuclear power, since it is far safer than any other kind in use. The hosts did not want that either. {078-J09}
## Invisible infrastructure

Then Varma pressed Shah. India, he worried, lacks the invisible infrastructure, the better rule of law and processes honed over decades, that lets such models work in the West. The state might hand the sector to a crony, botch the security, or turn any small role into rent-seeking.

Shah called these fair concerns and admitted the path would be difficult. His answer, from their episode *The Long Road to Change*, is a vibrant intellectual landscape of thinkers, researchers and critics that pulls a fumbling state back whenever it goes too far either way. {078-C13}
~ “Out of that,” he said, “we become a better country.”

quote.text: The answer lies in knowledge and community that we need enough people in India who think, who write, who debate, who criticise.

side.boxText: Everything Ajay Shah reported, he said, was joint work with his co-author Akshay Jaitly. Their article on it came out, Amit Varma noted, in practically the same week that Meta and Google placed big orders for small modular reactors. {078-J14}

contQuote.text: We are not arguing for action. We are arguing for freedom, that this is incredible. Let’s not shut it out with state action that gets in the way.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: U-boats, Tiger tanks, a bomb built from scratch and a ministry’s early calculations

stories.start: So I'm going to fly back to nineteen forty one
stories.end: was bigger than any submarines that Germany could put into the sea
stories.caption: the ugly duckling ships
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the Battle of the Atlantic, and what it teaches
stories.head: You sink them, we’ll build more
body: “All the great stories of the world begin at the Second World War,” Ajay Shah announced, and flew back to 1941. {078-J02}

The Battle of the Atlantic was under way. German submarines, the so-called U-boats, were sinking the ships that carried food, weapons and military supplies from America to Britain. Britain was an island: cut its link to America, and you strangled its ability to resist.
Hundreds of ships were lost. The hosts reached for a Bob Dylan song and asked how many ships the U-boats must shoot down before the British have no food. {078-J03}

The answer began with a mediocre British design of about ten thousand tons, affectionately called the ugly duckling. Ships had always been artisanal: people put the pieces together bit by bit, and each one came out different. The Americans decided to mass-produce this one, Henry Ford style, on assembly lines at 18 shipyards. {#shipyards}
Then came the gains from learning. At the beginning it took 270 days to commission a ship; by the end, it took 35. {#shipdays} In all, 2,700 ships were built, and the price crashed.

The message to the Germans, as Shah put it: “You keep shooting down our ships, we’ll make even more of the ships.” {078-S02} Mighty American manufacturing was bigger than any submarines Germany could put into the sea.

~ Shah thinks the battle is underrated: one of the most interesting stories of the war, about how ingenuity, effort, imagination and creativity came together. Perhaps, he said, it deserves an episode of its own.
stories.why: Scale and the learning curve beat craftsmanship. Shah’s point is that nuclear power can get cheap the same way: build small reactors by the thousand on assembly lines, instead of one-off giant plants. {078-C07}

stories.start: Similarly, there is a story around tanks. Uh the German Tiger Tank
stories.end: and they just like blew away German manufacturing by 10x
stories.caption: the Tiger and the Sherman
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on craftsmen, assembly lines and the Tiger
stories.head: A tank too finely made
body: The German Tiger tank was a great tank, Ajay Shah said. Its trouble, he said, was that it was an artisanal product.

“Every eleven Tiger tanks that were produced, there would be a change in the design,” he said. “Because the people making those tanks were master craftsmen. And that’s dumb. It drives up the cost.” {078-S03}
What you want, Shah said, is a factory that just mass-produces the design. The Americans did that with the Sherman tank, and then taught the Soviets how to do it with the T-34.
~ Together, he said, they blew away German manufacturing by a factor of ten. It was the same lesson as the ships, and the one Shah would apply to nuclear reactors.
stories.why: Constant tinkering by experts is the enemy of cost reduction. A standardised, good-enough design, produced at volume, wins wars, and Shah argues it can win markets for nuclear reactors too.

stories.start: all credit to the Indian nuclear science establishment that they got to
stories.end: This is not something that fits well in the Indian state.
stories.caption: India’s 1974 nuclear test
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on India’s 1974 test, and why power is different
stories.head: The bomb India built alone
body: Most nuclear powers got there through leaks, Ajay Shah said. The Soviets stole secrets from the Manhattan Project; the Soviets passed them to the Chinese, and the Chinese to the North Koreans and the Pakistanis.

India was different. It went from scratch to a nuclear test in 1974, without any proliferation. Shah credited the glory days of Homi Bhabha, Raja Ramanna, Sethna and their colleagues. “More power to them,” he said. {078-S04}
But building efficient, cheap nuclear energy, he said, is a different problem, closer to the work of Bharat Heavy Electricals: an ordinary industrial problem of scale and unit economics.

~ “This is not something that fits well in the Indian state,” Shah said. India assumed everything nuclear belonged to the Department of Atomic Energy, he argued, and nuclear’s share has stayed minuscule.

quote.text: India is one of the few countries which figured this out entirely alone.

stories.start: And uh I remember when I was at the Ministry of Finance.
stories.end: reactors are very, very cost efficient compared with what happens here.
stories.caption: the numbers at the Finance Ministry
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s early sums at the Ministry of Finance
stories.head: A reactor that failed the sums
body: When Ajay Shah was at the Ministry of Finance, he started on some early calculations about India’s government-run nuclear power plants. They told him, he said, “that this isn’t going anywhere”. {078-S05}
Measure the cost correctly, he found, and there was just no way those plants could play a meaningful role in the Indian energy mix. The efficiency was not there.
Even then it was clear, Shah said, that the top-of-the-line French and American reactors were very, very cost efficient compared with what happened here.

~ The share of nuclear energy in Indian energy consumption, he said, remains minuscule and has not grown over the years. In his dream, foreign firms would sell reactors to private Indian buyers, with Indian engineering firms joining them after five, ten or twenty years. {#dream}
stories.why: The trouble with Indian nuclear power was never only the fear of accidents. A state monopoly, Shah argued, simply could not deliver competitive economics, which is why he wants the decisions left to private firms. {078-C08}

quiz.q: Who called a meeting around the sentence “The Japanese are as good as us”?
quiz.a: Angela Merkel, after Fukushima; Germany then shut down all its nuclear power.

quiz.q: How did Shah sum up the American answer to the U-boats?
quiz.a: “You keep shooting down our ships, we’ll make even more of the ships.”

quiz.q: Why did Germany’s Tiger tank cost so much, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: Master craftsmen changed its design after every eleven tanks produced.

quiz.q: In what year did India conduct its nuclear test, and how unusually?
quiz.a: 1974, and it figured it out entirely alone, with no leaked secrets.

quiz.q: Why does the sun pose a problem for a solar power system, in Shah’s telling?
quiz.a: It sets every evening, just as people get home and switch things on.

quiz.q: Under the international doctrine, whom do victims of a nuclear accident sue?
quiz.a: Only the operator, who alone may then sue the vendor over design defects.
